assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's realisation turned optical lattice clocks into the most precise measurement devices ever built, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The work rests on a clean piece of atomic physics: engineering the light shift so that atoms in a lattice are probed without perturbation. It opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift in the laboratory, and a path to redefining the second. This is the kind of precision atomic physics where theory and experiment meet in detail.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice in 2001-2003 and demonstrated early strontium clocks; Ye's JILA group brought the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability. Two laureates give a clear and fair configuration. Ion-clock and frequency-comb work is already recognised (2005, 2012) and is not part of this candidate. Other strontium and ytterbium groups contributed refinements, but not the decisive ideas.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, and clock comparisons agree. The redefinition of the second is still pending, but the science is long settled and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: I have not verified the exact present record uncertainties and rely on memory.
A committee might ask whether the prize should also cover ion clocks or the frequency comb link, which would complicate the allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models in a controlled way: the superfluid-to-Mott transition, single-site imaging through quantum-gas microscopes, and quantum simulation of many-body states. It lets us ask genuine many-body questions that no classical computer can answer, using a system we understand atom by atom. This is fundamental physics with a clear conceptual message, and it follows the earlier BEC recognition (2001).
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) supplied the proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model with cold atoms; Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott insulator in 2002 and built the field, and Greiner's quantum-gas microscope was a decisive step. Cirac is also credited and has an equally strong case, so choosing three of four names means leaving out a major theorist. Gross, Bakr and other microscope pioneers, and Jaksch, are not in the credited set.
assessment.maturity: Mature in its core results, reproduced across many laboratories worldwide. The programme is still expanding (fermionic Hubbard physics, quantum magnetism), and the strongest scientific claims about quantum advantage in simulation are still developing, but the foundational discoveries are firm.
uncertainties: Whether Cirac should replace or join the theorists is unresolved, and the three-name limit forces a hard choice.
Overlap with the separate Cirac-Zoller candidate (B031) could split support.
I rely on my own recollection of who did what in 1998-2010.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses the wave nature of matter to make measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants (h/m, the fine-structure constant) at very high precision. It is a direct and beautiful use of quantum mechanics and has tested the equivalence principle and general relativity in new ways. It follows from laser cooling (1997) and links the quantum nature of matter to metrology.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made early matter-wave interferometers with atoms and built the physics of atom optics; Bordé laid out the theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry and its sensitivity to inertial effects; Kasevich (with Chu) demonstrated light-pulse atom interferometry and the atomic gravimeter and gyroscope. Chu has already shared a prize and is not credited here, which keeps the configuration clean, though others (Chu, Rasel, Peters) also have a claim.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of independent confirmation and working gravimeters and clocks; the large-scale tests (long baselines, space missions) are still maturing, but the basic discovery is settled.
uncertainties: Credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu is partly arbitrary and may be disputed.
A committee might judge it more as technique than as a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling a mechanical oscillator to its quantum ground state and controlling it with light or microwaves moves quantum mechanics into objects with billions of atoms. It speaks directly to the question I care about most, where the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds lies. The work also gives practical sensors and quantum transducers, though this was not the original motivation.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (with O'Connell, Martinis) showed the first mechanical quantum ground state in 2010; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer led the optomechanical cavity-cooling and strong-coupling work and quantum control with light. Teufel, Lehnert and Painter, who also reached the ground state through other approaches, are not credited, so the allocation is not complete and some claims could be contested.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for ground-state cooling and quantum-limited measurement, with several independent platforms confirming the results. Tests of macroscopic superposition and gravity-related ideas are still ahead, so the part that would most interest me is not yet established. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in theme, and committee members may feel that area was just recognised.
uncertainties: Possible thematic overlap with the 2025 prize.
The set of credited names omits several pioneers who also reached the ground state.
I have not independently checked priority dates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyons are quasiparticles with exchange statistics that are neither bosonic nor fermionic. The prediction was a surprising piece of fundamental theory, and its experimental establishment in fractional quantum Hall systems shows that quantum statistics in two dimensions is richer than we assumed. That is a genuine conceptual discovery about nature, and it is the basis for proposals in topological quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim made the 1977 prediction of intermediate statistics in two dimensions; Wilczek (not credited) coined the name anyon and added key work, and Haldane and Halperin/Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek also contributed. On the experimental side, Heiblum's group did the first fractional-charge shot-noise measurements and interferometers, Fève's group made the anyon collider, and Manfra's samples enabled the interferometers. With six credited names and notable omissions, a fair configuration is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Partly mature. The fractional-charge results are well confirmed, and the statistics were demonstrated in 2020 by two independent experiments (colliders and interferometers), but non-abelian statistics are not yet established and interpretation of some interferometry results is still debated. Recognition could be slightly early, though the abelian case is already robust.
uncertainties: Credit among the theory pioneers and the omission of Wilczek and others is unresolved.
Interpretation of the interferometry experiments is still discussed in the community.
I defer to condensed matter colleagues on the detailed experimental assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal showed how trapped ions could carry out quantum logic and how cold atoms could simulate quantum many-body systems. Their ideas shaped a whole field of quantum optics and gave experimentalists a concrete route to controlled quantum information processing. I value it as deep theory that was translated into working experiments by others.
assessment.attribution: The two are a natural pair, and the credit is clean for the theory itself. Experimental realisation belongs to ion-trap groups (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe), with Wineland already recognised in 2012, so the prize would honour theory that guided experiment. Overlap with B041 on the quantum-simulation side may lead to competing claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the ion-trap gate and many quantum-simulation proposals have been implemented and reproduced in many laboratories. The recognition is arguably overdue for the theory, but the 2012 prize and the 2022 prize on entanglement already cover part of the ground.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with prior prizes (2012, 2022) and with B041.
A theory-only prize may be less compelling to colleagues who weigh experimental discovery more strongly.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire gain media and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorbers) made reliable femtosecond lasers possible. They are the working tool behind attosecond physics, frequency combs and ultrafast spectroscopy, so their importance for my own field is large. Still, it is an enabling invention, and I personally prefer a prize for a discovery about nature. Chirped-pulse amplification (2018) and attosecond pulses (2023) have already been recognised.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire laser, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking, and Keller's SESAMs made self-starting passive mode-locking robust. Spence and others also contributed, and credit within Kerr-lens mode-locking is a known sensitive question. I should state that Keller is a close collaborator of my group, which I would need to weigh carefully in any recusal discussion.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, in use in laboratories everywhere for decades, so timing is not an issue. The risk is that the committee may see it as an incremental part of an already recognised ultrafast story.
uncertainties: Conflict of interest through collaboration with Keller.
Kerr-lens mode-locking priority between Sibbett's group and others is not fully settled in my memory.
Whether this is a discovery or primarily an invention for the purposes of the prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection of single nitrogen-vacancy centres and coherent control of their spins made a robust room-temperature quantum system, now used for nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and quantum networks. It shows that a defect in a solid can behave like an isolated atom, which is a nice conceptual point, and the sensing results reach well beyond physics into biology and materials.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko performed the first single-NV optical detection and spin control in 1997 and 2004; Lukin's group built much of the quantum-sensing and multi-qubit work with NV centres, along with Awschalom, Hanson and others who are not credited. Allocation among the many strong groups is not obvious, and the credited trio may not capture the decisive set.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for single-spin detection and coherent control, widely reproduced. Quantum-sensing applications are still growing, and several headline claims, such as practical advantage in biological sensing, are still evolving.
uncertainties: Credit among Awschalom, Hanson and the credited trio is contested.
Whether the discovery is distinct enough from the technology it enabled.
I rely on my own memory of priority dates.
